design_detail: Secondary analysis of the 2007 Australian National Survey of Mental Health and Wellbeing (NSMHWB; 8,841 respondents aged 16–85; stratified multistage household probability sample; response 60%). For each of five substance classes (alcohol, cannabis, stimulants, sedatives, opioids), respondents who reported use and a valid age of first use form a subsample (stimulants: 579). Two quantities are reported: a descriptive conditional probability (the weighted share of the subsample with a lifetime DSM-IV use disorder, abuse or dependence, at interview) and a cumulative probability by years since first use from discrete-time survival analysis, in which people without a disorder are censored at their age at interview. Pre-existing mood, anxiety and substance use disorders enter the survival models as time-varying predictors.
can_establish: For Australians aged 16–85 in 2007 who reported having used stimulants (class not defined), the share who had ever met DSM-IV criteria for stimulant abuse or dependence, a projected cumulative probability of doing so by years since first use, and associations between earlier-onset disorders and the transition, all from one retrospective interview.
cannot_establish: A figure for methamphetamine (the paper names no drug in its stimulant class), a dependence-only figure comparable with older surveys, causal effects of pre-existing disorders on the transition (timing recalled at one interview), or differences between substances (the subsamples overlap and the authors state that direct comparison between substances was not possible).

sample.recruitment: Community household survey: stratified, multistage probability sample of households, one member aged 16–85 selected for the diagnostic interview; response rate 60% (p. 137).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Subsamples: respondents who reported using each substance and gave a valid age of first use. Excluded from the analysis: people who could not remember or refused an age of onset, or who dated disorder onset before first use (stimulants n = 6) (p. 137). Diagnostic criteria were asked only of people who had used a drug at least five times in their life (alcohol: frequency and quantity thresholds) (p. 137); the paper does not say whether people who used stimulants fewer than five times are in the subsample of 579.
sample.demographics: Stimulant subsample (weighted estimates): mean age 32.6 (95% CI 31.5–33.6); 65.0% men; 6.8% unemployed; 85.3% born in Australia; 77.4% completed year 12 or higher; family history of alcohol or drug problems 28.6%; lifetime anxiety disorder 47.4%, affective disorder 31.4%, any substance use disorder 77.7%, any mental disorder 86.6% (Table 1, p. 139).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview); 40% of selected households did not respond (p. 137).
sample.selection_effects: Household frame (people in institutions or without a home are not sampled); a 60% response with no non-response analysis reported here; survivors only (people who died before 2007 cannot be interviewed); the substance subsamples overlap, because use of several substances was common (p. 138; Table 1 note).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported lifetime use and exact age of first use in a modified WMH-CIDI 3.0, with recall probes linking first use to developmental milestones (p. 137).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured beyond lifetime use; the diagnostic section required at least five occasions of drug use (p. 137). Frequency, route and duration are not analysed.
exposure.polysubstance: Common and not excluded (subsamples not mutually exclusive); earlier use of, and earlier disorders for, other substances enter the survival models as time-varying covariates (p. 138; Table 2).

comparison.controls: No separate comparison group: within each subsample, the survival models compare person-years of people who did and did not go on to develop the disorder.
comparison.matching: Not applicable. All models controlled for age, sex, education, age of first use, family history of alcohol or drug problems, number of comorbid mental disorders with earlier onset and number of other substance use disorders with earlier onset (p. 138; Table 2 note).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Socioeconomic status, area-level deprivation and externalizing spectrum disorders were not examined, as the authors note (p. 141); childhood adversity is not included.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Other substance use and disorders are covariates, not exclusions.

outcomes.instruments: Modified WMH-CIDI 3.0: lifetime DSM-IV abuse or dependence for each substance class, with age of onset taken as the earliest onset of either; DSM-IV mood and anxiety disorders without hierarchy rules; lifetime daily tobacco use (p. 137).
outcomes.validity_norms: The instrument is described as calibrated against the SCID-IV (p. 137). No biological or record verification; ages of first use and of onset are recalled retrospectively, in some cases over decades.
outcomes.operationalization: Use disorder = DSM-IV abuse or dependence (not dependence alone). Time at risk starts at first use for drugs and at the first year with more than 12 standard drinks for alcohol (p. 137).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate across covariates; bold type in Table 2 marks associations significant after correction (p. 138; Table 2 note).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive conditional probability of a lifetime use disorder: stimulants 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8), opioids 44.7% (35.2–54.2), sedatives 39.0% (27.5–50.4), alcohol 34.5% (32.9–36.2), cannabis 31.8% (28.5–35.2); median age of onset of stimulant use disorder 20 years (IQR 18–24) (p. 138). Survival analysis: probability of a stimulant use disorder within the first year after first use 12.2%; cumulative 50.4% by 14 years after first use (data right-censored at 14 years; no interval given); half of the stimulant cases had onset about 3 years (IQR 1–5) after first use (p. 138). Predictors of stimulant use disorder significant after false-discovery-rate correction: generalized anxiety disorder OR 3.89 (2.01–7.53), PTSD 2.51 (1.58–3.99), any anxiety disorder 2.13 (1.35–3.36), earlier cannabis use disorder 7.03 (4.02–12.29), any other earlier substance use disorder 5.09 (3.26–7.94); not significant after correction although the interval excludes 1: sedative use 1.91 (1.08–3.40), opioid use disorder 2.37 (1.04–5.46) (Table 2, p. 140).
analysis.covariates: Age, sex, education, age of first use, family history, number of earlier comorbid mental disorders and number of earlier other substance use disorders (p. 138).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The year-by-year cumulative probabilities are only in a supplement, which was not read (p. 138). The abstract gives the survival figure (50.4%) but not the descriptive one (45.7%, with its interval).
analysis.power: The stimulant subsample (579) gives an interval of about ±6 points for the descriptive proportion; the authors note wide intervals for the sedative and opioid subsamples (p. 141).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 579 Australians who reported using stimulants, 45.7% (39.5–51.8) had ever met DSM-IV criteria for stimulant abuse or dependence by the interview; projecting over time since first use, the survival analysis estimated 50.4% by 14 years after first use, 12.2% within the first year, with half of the cases starting within about 3 years. The outcome includes abuse, the class is undefined, and all timing is recalled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that 50.4% of people who used stimulants would develop a use disorder (p. 136), and the conclusion that one-third to one-half of people who use substances go on to develop one, with the highest rates for stimulants and opioids (p. 141). Gaps: (1) the substances are ranked although the limitations say direct comparison between substances was not possible (p. 141); (2) the figure called a lifetime cumulative probability is truncated at 14 years after first use (p. 138); (3) the discussion describes the transition as from regular use (p. 139) while the analysis starts at first use for drugs (pp. 137–138); (4) odds ratios from the survival models are described as risk ('more than trebled the risk', p. 140); (5) the call for early identification of mood and anxiety disorders to prevent secondary use disorders (p. 141) rests on associations from recalled timing. The authors do say that their estimates are substantially higher than in other surveys and that counting abuse as well as dependence raises them (p. 139).

timeline.event: US National Comorbidity Survey: 11.2% of people who had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically had ever met DSM-III-R dependence criteria, a proportion at one interview among everyone who had ever used

Wittchen et al. (2008), as reported here: transitions from first use to abuse 9.6–38.6% and to dependence 4.6–17.9% across substances; abuse or dependence for other illicit drugs 23.2% in men and 16.1% in women (p. 140); not read
McBride et al. (2009), as reported here: conditional dependence higher in Australia than in the United States for all substances except alcohol (p. 139); not read
NESARC survival analysis of transition to dependence for nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine; no amphetamine or methamphetamine estimate

This survey analysis: stimulant use disorder (abuse or dependence) 45.7% at interview and 50.4% by 14 years after first use, which the authors describe as substantially higher than earlier estimates of about one in four (p. 139)

replication.where_it_stands: The only population estimate seen so far that reports a stimulant-specific cumulative probability by years since first use. Its figures are much higher than older dependence-only proportions, and the authors attribute part of the difference to counting abuse and to Australian conditions; no survey reports a methamphetamine-specific figure, and none reproduces this one with the same measure.

funding.funder: The 2007 NSMHWB was funded by the Australian Government and conducted by the Australian Bureau of Statistics; the NHMRC Centre of Research Excellence in Mental Health and Substance Use is funded by the National Health and Medical Research Council; the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre is supported by the Australian Government under the Substance Misuse Prevention and Service Improvements Grants Fund; NHMRC Fellowships to M. Teesson and K. Mills and a Society for Mental Health Research Fellowship to C. Marel (p. 141).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors are at the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre and the NHMRC Centre of Research Excellence in Mental Health and Substance Use, University of New South Wales (p. 136). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort followed from first use, separating methamphetamine from other stimulants, assessing DSM-5 use disorder (and dependence-level, moderate to severe, disorder separately) at fixed intervals, and reporting both the cumulative incidence by years since first use with intervals and the proportion affected at fixed follow-up times, in more than one country.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: National household frame of Australians aged 16–85; people in institutions and people without a home, among whom stimulant use disorders may be more common, are not sampled.
Stratified multistage probability sample with sampling weights, replicate weights and jackknife standard errors (pp. 137–138).
579 people in the stimulant subsample give an interval of about ±6 points for the descriptive proportion; cells for individual predictors and later years since first use are small.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 describes each subsample, but the stimulant class is never defined and the 'weighted prevalence' row is not explained (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Exclusions for invalid ages are small (stimulants 6), but whether people who had used fewer than five times, who were not asked the diagnostic questions, are in the denominator is not stated.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: WMH-CIDI 3.0 DSM-IV diagnoses by structured interview, but self-report only, with ages of first use and onset recalled retrospectively (a limitation the authors state, p. 141) and coded by inconsistent rules (p. 137).

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same instrument and algorithm for all respondents.

Discrete-time survival analysis with time-varying covariates, design-based standard errors and false-discovery-rate control is appropriate, but the cumulative probabilities have no intervals, the 'lifetime' figure is truncated at 14 years, and two different probabilities are given for the same transition without explaining how they differ.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Response 60%, described as comparable with other national surveys; weights are applied, but no non-response analysis is reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large national probability survey with a standard diagnostic interview and an appropriate survival framework. What limits its numbers for this encyclopedia is less bias than scope: the stimulant class is undefined, the outcome includes DSM-IV abuse, the time at risk and the onset are recalled at one interview, and the denominator may or may not include people who used only a few times. It may be cited for the share of Australians who had used stimulants who had ever had a stimulant use disorder (abuse or dependence) and for the projected cumulative probability by years since first use, each labelled as such; not for methamphetamine specifically, not as a dependence figure, and not to rank substances.

key_findings.finding: Data from the 2007 Australian NSMHWB: 8,841 respondents aged 16–85 from a stratified multistage household probability sample, response 60%. Subsamples with valid age of first use: alcohol 5,456, cannabis 1,629, stimulants 579, opioids 156, sedatives 137; the subsamples are not independent.

Diagnostic criteria were asked only of people who had used a drug at least five times in their life; lifetime DSM-IV abuse or dependence was assessed with a modified WMH-CIDI 3.0, and the age of onset of the disorder was the earliest age of onset of either abuse or dependence.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1. Sample, 2nd paragraph; Methods › 2.2. Measures, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Conditional probability of a lifetime use disorder (descriptive): stimulants 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8), opioids 44.7% (35.2–54.2), sedatives 39.0% (27.5–50.4), alcohol 34.5% (32.9–36.2), cannabis 31.8% (28.5–35.2); median age of onset of stimulant use disorder 20 years (IQR 18–24).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2.1. Discrete Time Survival Analysis, 3rd paragraph; Methods › 2.3. Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The Methods describe these as descriptive estimates for each subsample, although they are printed under the survival-analysis heading.

key_findings.finding: Survival analysis for stimulants: data right-censored at 14 years after first use; probability of a use disorder within the first year after first use 12.2%; cumulative probability 50.4% within an estimated 14 years after first use; half of the stimulant cases had onset about 3 years (IQR 1–5) after first use. No intervals are given for the cumulative probabilities, and the year-by-year values are in a supplement (not read).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2.1. Discrete Time Survival Analysis, 1st paragraph; Results › 3.3. Cumulative conditional probability and speed of transitioning, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cumulative incidence curves from first use to disorder are shown for each class; values were not extracted beyond those given in the text.

Predictors of the transition from stimulant use to stimulant use disorder, significant after false-discovery-rate correction: generalized anxiety disorder OR 3.89 (2.01–7.53), PTSD 2.51 (1.58–3.99), any anxiety disorder 2.13 (1.35–3.36), earlier cannabis use disorder 7.03 (4.02–12.29), any other earlier substance use disorder 5.09 (3.26–7.94). Major depressive episode 1.25 (0.73–2.13) was not associated.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.4.1. Psychiatric predictors, 2nd paragraph; Results › 3.4.2. Substance use predictors, 2nd paragraph (pp. 138–139); Table 2, stimulant use disorder column (p. 140)

key_findings.finding: The authors write that their estimates are substantially higher than in other surveys, where the highest cumulative probabilities had been around one in four for cocaine, opioids and alcohol; that most earlier studies counted dependence without abuse and so give lower estimates; and that earlier comparative work found higher conditional dependence in Australia than in the United States.

Limitations stated by the authors: retrospective recall of ages of first use and onset; small sedative and opioid subsamples; overlapping subsamples, so that direct comparison between substances was not possible; socioeconomic status, area-level deprivation and externalizing disorders not examined.

Stimulant subsample characteristics: weighted prevalence 3.3% (2.8–3.9); mean age 32.6; 65.0% men; lifetime any substance use disorder 77.7%; lifetime any mental disorder 86.6%; 12-month substance use disorder 28.8%.
The stimulant class is not defined anywhere in the paper; no drug (amphetamine, methamphetamine, cocaine, ecstasy) is named as belonging to it.
key_findings.locator: Whole text, including Methods › 2.2. Measures, 1st paragraph (p. 137)
key_findings.note: Editors' observation from reading the whole text.

reporting_issues.issue: Two different probabilities are given for the same transition: 45.7% (95% CI 39.5–51.8), described in the Methods as a descriptive estimate (p. 138), and 50.4% (no interval) from the survival analysis (p. 138); the abstract and conclusion use only the second (pp. 136, 141), and the paper never explains how the two differ.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader can mistake one for the other; the descriptive share at interview and the projected cumulative probability by 14 years must be cited separately.

reporting_issues.issue: The figure called a lifetime cumulative probability is truncated at 14 years after first use, the point beyond which no stimulant onsets were observed (p. 138).
reporting_issues.consequence: It is a cumulative probability by 14 years after first use, not over a lifetime.

reporting_issues.issue: The denominator is ambiguous: diagnostic criteria were asked only of people who had used a drug at least five times (p. 137), but the paper does not say whether people with fewer uses are in the stimulant subsample of 579.
reporting_issues.consequence: If they are excluded, the probabilities are conditional on more than occasional use and cannot be compared with figures among everyone who ever used.

reporting_issues.issue: The rules for coding age of first use conflict: first use before age 14 is bottom-coded at 13 in Methods 2.1, while first use before the teens is coded at 12, before the twenties at 19 and after the twenties at 20 in Methods 2.2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the coding affects the time from first use to onset, not the shares with a disorder.

reporting_issues.issue: The first row of Table 1, 'Weighted prevalence (%)', is not defined. Read as the prevalence of use, it conflicts with the subsample sizes (stimulants 3.3% against 579 of 8,841 = 6.5% unweighted; alcohol 22.1% against 61.7%); divided by the conditional probabilities it gives 7.2% for stimulants, 64.1% for alcohol and 19.5% for cannabis, close to the unweighted shares, so it is probably the weighted prevalence of the use disorder (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The row should not be cited as the prevalence of stimulant use in Australia.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says the study estimated the transition from regular use to use disorder (p. 139), while for drugs the time at risk starts at first use (pp. 137–138); section 3.4 is headed transition to dependence although the outcome is abuse or dependence (p. 138).
reporting_issues.consequence: Inconsistent labels for both the starting point and the outcome.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says only an earlier sedative use disorder significantly increased the transition to opioid use disorder (p. 141), but Table 2 also marks any other earlier substance use disorder (OR 5.57, 1.93–16.07) as significant for opioids (p. 140).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor and not about stimulants; text and table disagree.

reporting_issues.issue: Odds ratios from discrete-time survival models are described as multiples of risk ('more than trebled the risk', p. 140).
reporting_issues.consequence: The wording overstates what an odds ratio of the yearly transition shows.
